To find $(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{3}),$ we need to find the number that is located in row $6$ and position $3$ of Pascal's triangle. 

**Important**: When counting the rows and positions in Pascal's triangle, we always start counting from zero! Remember:

- The top row of Pascal's triangle is row $0.$

- The first position of each row (the one of the left) is position number $0.$

The location of $(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{3})$ in Pascal's triangle is highlighted below.

$$
\begin{aligned} &  &  &  &  &  &  &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{0}{0}) \\  &  &  &  &  &  &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{1}{0}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{1}{1}) \\  &  &  &  &  &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{2}{0}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{2}{1}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{2}{2}) \\  &  &  &  &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{0}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{1}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{2}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{3}) \\  &  &  &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{0}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{1}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{2}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{3}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{4}) \\  &  &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{0}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{1}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{2}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{3}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{4}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{5}) \\  &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{0}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{1}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{2}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{3}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{4}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{5}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{6}) \\  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

Now, $(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{3})$ is the sum of the two closest numbers located in the previous row. So,

$$
(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{3})=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{2})+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{3})
$$

Therefore, the missing expression is $(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{3}).$
